s: The ask is the highest price a buyer is willing to pay.
why: That's the bid. The ask (or offer) is the lowest price a seller will accept.

s: A wide bid-ask spread usually means a stock is harder to trade cheaply.
why: Each round trip costs you about the spread, so wide spreads mean costly, less liquid trading.

s: The last traded price is the price you are guaranteed to get on your next market order.
why: A market order fills at the best available ask or bid, which can differ from the last trade.

s: In a liquid stock you can trade a large quantity without moving the price much.
why: That is what liquidity means: size trades cheaply and quickly.

s: Volume counts buyers and sellers separately, so 100 shares changing hands is volume of 200.
why: Every trade has a buyer and a seller; 100 shares traded is volume of 100.

s: Ten lakh make one million.
why: 1 lakh = 1,00,000, so 10 lakh = 10,00,000 = one million.

s: One crore equals one billion.
why: One crore is ten million. 100 crore make one billion.

s: A company's market cap rises when it takes on more debt.
why: Market cap is share price × shares outstanding; debt isn't in it (enterprise value adds debt).

s: A rate going from 6.50% to 6.75% is a rise of 25 basis points.
why: One basis point is 0.01%, so 0.25% is 25 bps.

s: You have a position only while an order is waiting to be filled.
why: An open order isn't a position. A position is what you actually hold after a fill.

s: Being long a stock means you gain if its price rises.
why: Long means you own it (or are exposed as if you did), so you profit from a rise.

s: Margin is a fee the broker keeps for letting you trade.
why: Margin is money blocked as collateral against losses; you get it back when you close.

s: P&L includes both closed trades and positions still open, unless it says realised or unrealised.
why: Plain P&L is the total; realised and unrealised split it.

s: Unrealised profit becomes realised when the price moves in your favour.
why: It's realised only when you close the position; until then it's on paper.

s: Marking to market can show a loss on a position you haven't sold.
why: MTM revalues open positions at today's price, so paper losses show up daily.

s: The notional of a futures position is the margin you paid for it.
why: Notional is the full value controlled (price × quantity); margin is a fraction of it.

s: With 5x leverage, a 4% fall in price is about a 20% loss on your own capital.
why: Leverage multiplies both gains and losses: 5 × 4% = 20%.

s: A gain of 50% followed by a loss of 50% leaves you back where you started.
An investment that doubles in 5 years has a CAGR of about 15%, not 20%.
why: 2^(1/5) − 1 ≈ 14.9%. 20% would be simple, not compounded.

s: A highly volatile stock is one whose price only falls.
why: Volatility measures how much prices swing, up and down, not the direction.

s: A company can pay a dividend even in a year it makes a loss, out of past reserves.
why: Dividends can come from accumulated profits, though it's a warning sign if sustained.

s: If a stock's price falls and its dividend stays the same, its dividend yield falls.
why: Yield = dividend ÷ price, so a lower price means a higher yield.

s: Total return can be positive even when the share price ends lower, if dividends cover the fall.
why: Total return adds dividends to the price change.

s: A share's face value tells you roughly what it trades for on the exchange.
why: Face value is a nominal figure (often ₹1 or ₹10) and has little to do with market price.

s: A company's book value can be negative if its liabilities exceed its assets.
why: Book value is assets minus liabilities, which can go below zero.

s: Fair value is the price the stock last traded at.
why: Fair value is an estimate of worth; the market price may sit above or below it.

s: A stock trading at a premium to its peers has a higher valuation multiple than them.
why: Premium means priced above the reference, here the peer group's multiple.

s: A stock at a discount to its fair value is always a good buy.
why: It might be cheap for a reason; a discount is only a comparison, not a verdict.

s: If a stock is ₹800 and the target is ₹1,000, the upside is 25%.
EPS goes up whenever a company issues new shares.
why: Issuing shares spreads the same profit over more shares, which lowers EPS.

s: A P/E of 25 means you pay ₹25 for each ₹1 of yearly earnings.
why: P/E = price ÷ earnings per share.

s: A P/B below 1 means the company is losing money.
why: P/B below 1 means the market values it under its book value; it says nothing directly about profit.

s: Two companies with the same market cap can have very different enterprise values.
why: EV adds debt and subtracts cash, which differ between companies.

s: EBITDA is the cash that is left for shareholders after all expenses.
why: EBITDA is before interest, tax, depreciation and capex, so it overstates what's left for shareholders.

s: An EV/EBITDA of 12x is a valuation multiple.
why: A multiple is any ratio of value to a profit or sales figure.

s: In India, earnings season comes once a year.
why: Listed companies report quarterly, so there are four results seasons a year.

s: A company can beat analysts' estimates and still fall if it cuts its guidance.
why: The market prices the future; a weaker outlook can outweigh a good quarter.

s: Consensus is the forecast of the single most accurate analyst.
why: Consensus is the average (or median) of all covering analysts' forecasts.

s: A great company can be a poor investment if its valuation is too high.
why: Price paid matters: an expensive stock can disappoint even if the business does well.

s: A perfect hedge increases your profit if the market moves your way.
why: A hedge offsets moves both ways; it gives up gains to cut losses.

s: A portfolio can hold cash, bonds and gold as well as shares.
why: A portfolio is all of an investor's holdings, across asset classes.

s: A fund that falls 5% has underperformed its benchmark by 5%.
why: If the benchmark fell 8%, the fund outperformed by 3%. Compare against the benchmark's return.

s: A stock can fall in price and still outperform the market.
why: Outperform is relative: falling 2% while the index falls 6% is outperformance.

s: An analyst's "underperform" rating means the stock is expected to fall.
why: It means doing worse than the market or peers, which can still be a rise.

s: Buying a Nifty future gives you exposure to the index without owning its 50 stocks.
why: Exposure is how much you gain or lose from a move, however it's held.

s: Large caps and small caps are different asset classes.
why: Both are equities, one asset class; they are different segments within it.

s: NSE handles the vast majority of India's equity derivatives trading.
why: NSE dominates F&O volumes; BSE's share has grown but is smaller.

s: The Nifty 50 is BSE's flagship index.
why: BSE runs the Sensex. Nifty 50 belongs to NSE.

s: When you buy shares for delivery, you trade in the cash segment.
why: The cash (equity) segment is where shares themselves are bought and sold.

s: F&O trading in India is open only to institutions.
why: Retail traders can trade F&O through their broker, subject to margin and risk disclosures.

s: Promoter holding is disclosed every quarter in the shareholding pattern.
why: Listed companies file their shareholding pattern quarterly, promoters included.

s: Free float includes shares held by the promoters.
why: Free float excludes promoter and other locked-in holdings; it's what the public can trade.

s: Nifty 50 weights its stocks by free-float market cap.
why: Bigger free-float companies carry more weight in the index.

s: The Sensex is made up of 50 stocks.
why: The Sensex has 30 stocks. Nifty 50 has 50.

s: Bank Nifty is made up only of bank stocks.
why: It tracks the most liquid large banks listed on NSE.

s: Large cap means any company worth more than ₹10,000 crore.
why: In India it's the top 100 by full market cap, as ranked under SEBI's rules.

s: A company ranked 150th by market cap is a mid cap.
why: Mid caps are ranked 101 to 250.

s: Small caps are companies ranked 101 to 250 by market cap.
why: That's mid cap. Small caps are ranked 251 and below.

s: SEBI regulates stockbrokers, mutual funds and stock exchanges.
why: SEBI is the securities market regulator for all of these.

s: RBI is the regulator of stock exchanges.
why: RBI is the central bank (rates, banks, currency). SEBI regulates exchanges.

s: You need a registered stockbroker to buy shares on NSE.
why: Only exchange members can place orders; retail investors go through a broker.

s: Your shares are held by your stockbroker in its own name.
why: Shares sit in your demat account with a depository (NSDL or CDSL), in your name.

s: A demat account holds your shares; a trading account is used to place orders.
why: They're separate accounts with different jobs, usually opened together.

s: A depository participant is the exchange where your shares trade.
why: A DP is the agent (often your broker or bank) that runs your demat account with a depository.

s: You can't hold shares in a trading account; it is for placing orders.
why: Holdings sit in the demat account.

s: If the other side of your trade defaults, your trade is cancelled.
why: The clearing corporation steps in as the counterparty and guarantees settlement.

s: Shares bought on a Friday under T+1 normally reach your demat account on Monday.
why: T+1 counts working days, so Friday's trade settles the next working day, Monday.

s: STT is charged only when you make a profit.
why: STT is charged on the value of each eligible trade, profit or loss.

s: A contract note lists your trades with their prices, charges and taxes.
why: It's the legal record your broker sends after each trading day.

s: FPIs can only invest in Indian government bonds, not shares.
why: FPIs invest heavily in Indian shares, and also in bonds.

s: Mutual funds and insurers count as DIIs.
why: DIIs are domestic institutions: MFs, insurers, banks and pension funds.

s: Every individual investor counts as retail, however large the application.
why: In IPOs, individuals applying for more than ₹2 lakh are classed as HNIs (NIIs), not retail.

s: An individual applying for ₹5 lakh of shares in an IPO falls in the HNI (NII) category.
why: Applications above ₹2 lakh move from the retail quota to the NII quota.

s: A mutual fund guarantees you won't lose money.
why: Mutual funds carry market risk; their value goes up and down with what they hold.

s: A SIP buys more units when the NAV is low and fewer when it is high.
why: A fixed amount buys more units at lower prices; that's rupee-cost averaging.

s: A fund with a lower NAV is cheaper and so better value.
why: NAV is just per-unit value; a low NAV doesn't make a fund cheap.

s: An AMC can run many different mutual fund schemes.
why: The AMC is the fund house; each scheme is a separate fund it manages.

s: Every stock in India, including those with F&O, has a fixed daily circuit limit.
why: Stocks in F&O have no fixed price band; they use dynamic price bands instead.

s: A stock stuck at lower circuit can have many sellers and almost no buyers.
why: Trading continues only at the limit price, so sellers queue unfilled.

s: A market-wide circuit breaker halts just the stock that fell most.
why: It halts trading across all equity and equity derivatives on the exchanges.

s: Stocks under ASM can need higher margins, up to 100%.
why: ASM adds stricter rules such as higher margins to curb speculation.

s: Pre-open orders match continuously as they arrive.
why: Pre-open is a call auction: orders collect, then match at one price.

s: Muhurat trading takes place on Diwali.
why: It's a short, symbolic session held on Diwali evening for the new Samvat year.

s: A block deal can be done by any investor for any quantity.
why: Block deals have a minimum size and trade in a special window.

s: A bulk deal happens through normal market orders, not a special window.
why: It's a disclosure rule: one client trading over 0.5% of shares in a day.

s: In an IPO, all of the money always goes to the company.
why: In an offer-for-sale part, existing holders sell and get the money, not the company.

s: GMP is unofficial and isn't regulated by SEBI.
why: It comes from informal grey-market dealing, outside the exchanges.

s: Listing gains are guaranteed if an IPO is oversubscribed.
why: Strong demand helps, but the listing price can still fall below the issue price.

s: In an OFS, the company itself usually gets none of the money.
why: Existing shareholders are selling, so the proceeds go to them.

s: Retail investors can buy shares in a QIP.
why: A QIP is sold only to qualified institutional buyers.

s: Shareholders who skip a rights issue see their ownership share shrink.
why: New shares go to others, so your percentage falls.

s: To get the dividend, buying on the record date itself is enough.
why: Under T+1 the ex-date and record date are the same day, so you must buy at least one trading day before.

s: A buyback reduces the number of shares outstanding.
why: The company buys and cancels its own shares.

s: Most of India's commodity futures, including gold and crude oil, trade on MCX.
why: MCX is the main commodity derivatives exchange for bullion, metals and energy.

s: NCDEX is where India's crude oil and gold futures mainly trade.
why: Those trade on MCX. NCDEX focuses on farm commodities.

s: On MCX, gold is quoted per 10 grams and silver per kilogram.
why: Those are the standard quote units for the main contracts.

s: Gold and silver are base metals.
why: They're precious metals. Base metals are industrial: copper, zinc, aluminium, lead, nickel.

s: MCX crude oil prices move with both the global oil price and the rupee.
why: They're priced off WTI converted into rupees, so USDINR matters too.

s: MCX closes at 5 pm, like the equity market.
why: MCX trades till late at night, to overlap with US and European hours.

s: If USDINR rises while global gold is flat, Indian gold prices usually rise.
why: Import parity converts the global price at USDINR, so a weaker rupee lifts it.

s: A high convenience yield pushes futures prices further above spot.
why: Convenience yield lowers futures relative to spot, and can cause backwardation.

s: Storage costs are one reason commodity futures usually trade above spot.
why: Holding the physical good costs money, so later delivery is priced higher.

s: Super contango happens when storage is nearly empty.
why: It happens when storage is nearly full, making it very expensive to hold more.

s: A wider crack spread is usually good news for refiners.
why: It's a proxy for refining margin: product prices minus crude.

s: A gold-silver ratio of 85 means gold costs ₹85 more than silver.
why: It's a ratio: one ounce of gold buys about 85 ounces of silver.

s: A bigger-than-expected rise in US crude inventories usually pushes oil prices down.
why: More stored oil than expected signals weaker demand or more supply.

s: OPEC+ is made up only of Middle Eastern countries.
why: It includes non-OPEC allies such as Russia and Kazakhstan.

s: An in-the-money MCX option on futures can turn into a futures position at expiry.
why: That's devolvement: options on futures become the underlying futures contract.

s: A mini contract tracks a different, cheaper grade of the commodity.
why: It's the same commodity in a smaller lot size.

s: Exchanges can widen a commodity's daily price range after the limit is hit.
why: MCX relaxes the band in steps after a cooling-off period.

s: A hedger uses futures to make extra profit from price moves.
why: A hedger offsets an existing business exposure; the aim is protection, not profit.

s: Indian gold can trade at a discount to import parity when local demand is weak.
why: Dealers offer discounts in weak demand and charge premiums in strong demand.

s: A government bond in its own currency has almost no credit risk but still has interest-rate risk.
why: The government can pay in rupees, but rising rates still lower the bond's price.

s: A short-term bond loses more value than a long-term bond when rates rise.
why: Longer bonds have higher duration, so they lose more.

s: In India, a single day's delay on a rated bond's payment counts as a default.
why: Rating agencies treat even a one-day delay as default.

s: A AAA rating is a guarantee that the issuer won't default.
why: A rating is an opinion on likelihood, not a guarantee; AAA issuers have defaulted.

s: CRISIL and ICRA are credit rating agencies.
why: Both are SEBI-registered agencies, along with CARE and India Ratings.

s: A bond rated BB+ is investment grade.
why: Investment grade is BBB− or above. BB+ is high yield.

s: A corporate bond paying 8.5% when the same-maturity G-sec pays 7% has a spread of 150 bps.
A 2% probability of default means the investor will lose 2% of the bond's value each year.
why: It's the chance of default; the loss also depends on what's recovered.

s: Secured lenders usually recover more after a default than unsecured ones.
why: They have a claim on collateral, which raises recovery.

s: If the recovery rate is 40%, the loss given default is 40%.
why: LGD = 1 − recovery rate = 60%.

s: An NCD can't be converted into the company's shares.
why: That's what non-convertible means.

s: Commercial paper pays a coupon twice a year.
why: CP is issued at a discount and repaid at face value; there are no coupons.

s: A credit risk fund must put most of its money in bonds below the top ratings.
why: That's the category rule: higher yield for more default risk.

s: A segregated portfolio lets new investors share in any recovery from the defaulted bond.
why: Only investors holding units on the day of the split get recovery from the side pocket.

s: A rating watch can be negative, positive or developing.
why: It flags the likely direction of a possible change.

s: Breaking a covenant has no effect until the borrower misses a payment.
why: A covenant breach can let lenders demand early repayment or change terms.

s: You can buy CDS protection on a company without owning its bonds.
why: That's how CDS can be used to bet on credit, not just hedge.

s: Expected loss is the worst loss that can happen on a loan.
why: It's the average loss: PD × LGD × exposure. The worst case is far bigger.

s: High-yield bond prices tend to move more with the company's results than with interest rates.
why: Default risk dominates, so they behave a bit like equity.

s: Distressed debt always trades near its face value.
why: It trades at deep discounts, often under 50 paise on the rupee.

s: A bond's spread can look calm right up to a default.
why: Jump-to-default is a sudden gap, not a gradual slide.

s: When credit spreads widen, corporate bond prices rise relative to G-secs.
why: Wider spreads mean higher corporate yields, so their prices fall relative to G-secs.

s: A company can grow revenue and still post falling profit.
why: Costs or margins can fall faster than sales rise.

s: An EBITDA margin of 20% means the company keeps 20 paise of net profit from each rupee of sales.
why: It's operating profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, not net profit.

s: PAT can rise in a quarter even when operating profit falls, thanks to other income or lower tax.
why: PAT is after everything, so non-operating items can move it.

s: Comparing a December quarter with the September quarter is year-on-year growth.
why: That's quarter-on-quarter. Year-on-year compares with the December quarter last year.

s: Seasonal businesses can show big quarter-on-quarter swings that mean little.
why: Festive or monsoon seasons move sales between quarters, so YoY is cleaner.

s: High operating leverage means a company has borrowed a lot.
why: It's about fixed costs, not debt. That's financial leverage.

s: A jump in other income can flatter profit without the core business improving.
why: It comes from outside operations, such as interest on cash or investment gains.

s: Exceptional items are part of a company's recurring profit.
why: They're one-offs, reported separately so they can be stripped out.

s: A company can report profit while operating cash flow is negative.
why: Unpaid customer bills or growing inventory can tie up the cash.

s: Free cash flow is operating cash flow plus capex.
why: It's operating cash flow minus capex.

s: Capex shows up mostly as depreciation in the P&L over later years, not as a one-time expense.
why: It's capitalised as an asset and depreciated over its life.

s: A growing company usually needs less working capital as it grows.
why: More sales usually means more inventory and receivables, so more working capital.

s: Rising receivable days can mean customers are taking longer to pay.
why: Receivables ÷ sales × 365 goes up when collections slow.

s: Falling inventory days usually signal weakening demand.
why: Stock clearing faster usually means demand is healthy. Rising days are the worry.

s: Debt-to-equity of 2 means lenders fund twice as much as shareholders.
why: D/E = debt ÷ equity.

s: An interest coverage of 0.8x means interest is comfortably covered.
why: Below 1x, operating profit doesn't cover interest at all.

s: Borrowing more can raise ROE even if the business doesn't improve.
why: Debt shrinks equity relative to profit, which flatters ROE. That's why ROCE is checked too.

s: ROCE is flattered by borrowing in the same way as ROE.
why: ROCE counts debt in capital employed, so leverage doesn't inflate it.

s: Retailers usually have higher asset turnover than power utilities.
why: Retailers generate lots of sales per rupee of assets; utilities are asset-heavy.

s: A cash conversion of 40% of EBITDA is a sign of very high earnings quality.
why: Low conversion means much of the profit isn't turning into cash, which is a warning sign.

s: Profit driven by one-off gains is low-quality earnings.
why: Quality earnings come from the core business, in cash, repeatedly.

s: A stock split dilutes existing shareholders.
why: A split gives everyone more shares in proportion; ownership doesn't change.

s: A P/E of 30 with 30% expected earnings growth gives a PEG of 1.
why: PEG = P/E ÷ growth rate in percent = 30 ÷ 30 = 1.

s: EV/EBITDA ignores a company's debt.
why: EV includes net debt, which is why it compares companies with different debt levels.

s: NIM tends to rise for banks when their lending rates reprice faster than deposit rates.
why: NIM is interest earned minus interest paid, over earning assets.

s: A loan becomes an NPA as soon as one EMI is a day late.
why: A loan turns NPA when it's overdue for more than 90 days.

s: A higher CASA ratio usually means cheaper funding for a bank.
why: Current and savings accounts pay little interest compared with fixed deposits.

s: ARPU rises when a telecom company adds many low-paying users.
why: Low-paying users drag the average down. Tariff hikes or upgrades raise ARPU.

s: A retailer can grow total sales while same-store sales fall.
why: New store openings can lift total sales even if old stores sell less.

s: A large order backlog guarantees higher profit next year.
why: It's work in hand, but execution, costs and cancellations still decide profit.

s: High attrition raises hiring and training costs for an IT services firm.
why: People are the main cost, so replacing them is expensive.

s: TCV signed in a quarter is booked as revenue in that same quarter.
why: TCV is the whole-life value of deals; revenue comes over the years they run.

s: Consolidated results include the company's subsidiaries.
why: They add the parent and all subsidiaries together.

s: An investor presentation is a private document shared only with big funds.
why: It's filed on the exchange for everyone, usually with the results.

s: A stock can fall on strong numbers if management sounds cautious about the next quarters.
why: Markets price the outlook, and tone moves it.

s: Listed companies may choose not to disclose segment numbers.
why: Segment reporting is required with results for listed companies with distinct segments.

s: The shareholding pattern shows how much promoters have pledged.
why: It discloses promoter holdings and the share pledged.

s: A stock always rises when earnings grow strongly.
why: Stocks react to the surprise against expectations; strong growth below estimates can still fall.

s: Order inflow tells you about future revenue more than current-quarter revenue does.
why: Orders won now turn into revenue as they're executed.

s: The annual report's financial statements are unaudited.
why: Annual report statements are audited, with the auditor's report included.

s: The MD&A is where management explains performance and risks in its own words.
why: It's the narrative section of the annual report.

s: Notes to accounts only repeat the numbers in the main statements.
why: They explain policies, debt terms, guarantees and disputes the statements don't show.

s: Large related-party transactions need shareholder approval in India.
why: Material RPTs need approval from shareholders, with related parties not voting.

s: Contingent liabilities are shown as debt on the balance sheet.
why: They sit in the notes, because they depend on an event that may not happen.

s: A qualified audit opinion is more serious than an emphasis-of-matter paragraph.
why: Qualification means the auditor disagrees or couldn't verify; emphasis only highlights.

s: Companies don't have to explain why an auditor resigned.
why: They must file the reason with the exchange.

s: Hitting the bid means buying at the best price on offer.
why: Hitting the bid is selling at the best bid. Buying at the offer is lifting it.

s: Lifting the offer gets you filled fast but costs you the spread.
why: You buy at the seller's price straight away, paying up for speed.

s: A two-way price tells the other side which way you want to trade.
why: Showing both a bid and an offer hides your direction; that's the point of asking for one.

s: "Can you do size?" asks whether someone can trade a large quantity.
why: On the desk, size means quantity, and "in size" means a lot of it.

s: Working an order means sending the whole quantity to the market at once.
why: It means filling it in pieces over time so the price isn't pushed.

s: A big print in a stock tells traders a large trade has just gone through.
why: A print is a reported trade; large ones get watched closely.

s: Market color is the exchange's official data on prices and volumes.
why: Color is the informal context from brokers and traders: who's doing what, and why.

s: "Flow is better for sale" means more clients are selling than buying.
why: Flow is client orders through a desk; better for sale means sellers dominate.

s: A broker's axe is a position it is trying to hide from clients.
why: An axe is an interest the desk wants known, so it can find the other side.

s: A trader "running a book" is responsible for a set of positions and their risk.
why: The book is all the positions a trader or desk manages.

s: Brokers and investment banks are buy-side firms.
why: They're sell-side. Buy-side firms invest money: funds, insurers, pension funds.

s: A broker's research analyst works on the sell side.
why: Sell-side firms sell services, including research, to investors.

s: A fund manager places every order on the exchange personally.
why: The manager decides what to buy and sell; a dealer usually places the orders.

s: A research analyst can publish a sell rating on a stock.
why: Analysts give buy, hold or sell views on the companies they cover.

s: A sales trader manages the broker's own trading positions.
why: A sales trader takes clients' orders and shares color; prop traders run the firm's money.

s: In India, a fund's dealer is the person who places and manages its orders on the exchange.
why: The dealer executes what the fund manager decides.

s: An investment bank's main job is taking deposits from the public.
why: That's a commercial bank. Investment banks arrange share sales, debt and mergers.

s: A prop desk trades with the firm's own money, not clients'.
why: Proprietary trading is for the firm's own profit.

s: Hedge funds can only buy shares, never short them.
why: Hedge funds can short, use leverage and trade derivatives. Long-only funds can't.

s: A long-only fund can make money only when its holdings rise.
why: It can't short, so it gains only from rising prices.

s: A custodian decides which shares an institutional fund should buy.
why: A custodian holds securities and handles settlement; the fund manager decides.

s: "Initiating coverage" means an analyst publishes their first report on a company.
why: Coverage is the set of companies an analyst follows.

s: All Indian brokers use the same three ratings: buy, hold and sell.
why: Many also use add and reduce, and some use overweight and underweight.

s: A target price is usually set for about 12 months ahead.
why: Analysts commonly give a 12-month target.

s: Raising a target price always counts as an upgrade.
why: An upgrade is raising the rating, such as hold to buy; a higher target alone isn't one.

s: A stock can be downgraded from buy to hold even while its target price rises.
why: The rating and the target are separate; a smaller upside can cut the rating.

s: A fund that is overweight banks holds fewer banks than its benchmark.
why: Overweight means holding more than the benchmark's weight.

s: Analysts can question management directly on an earnings call.
why: The call has a Q&A where analysts and investors ask questions.

s: An earnings beat always makes the stock rise.
why: Stocks can fall on a beat if the quality, guidance or the whisper number disappoints.

s: A stock can rise sharply on a re-rating even if its earnings don't change.
why: A higher multiple on the same earnings lifts the price.

s: "Banks are well bid" means banks are falling as sellers rush out.
why: Well bid means buyers are eager and keep raising their bids.

s: "IT is offered" means sellers are in control of IT stocks.
why: Offered means sellers keep lowering their offers.

s: Chasing a stock gets you a better price than waiting.
why: You keep paying up as the market runs away, so you usually get a worse price.

s: Fading a gap-up means selling into it, expecting the price to fall back.
why: Fading is trading against a move you think will reverse.

s: Being stopped out means your profit target was hit.
why: It means your stop-loss was hit and you exited at a loss.

s: Trimming a position means selling part of it, not all.
why: Trim is a partial sale; selling everything is exiting or closing out.

s: Unwinding a trade means adding to it.
why: Unwinding is closing it out, often in steps.

s: Reading the tape means judging buying and selling pressure from live trades.
why: The tape is the live record of trades and prices.

s: In a principal trade, the broker takes no risk.
why: In a principal trade the broker trades from its own book and takes the risk; in an agency trade it doesn't.

s: In an agency trade, the broker earns a commission and takes no market risk.
why: It trades in the market on the client's behalf.

s: A firm price can be changed after you accept it.
why: A firm price is a commitment: accept it and the trade is done.

s: You can't hold a dealer to an indicative price.
why: It's a guide, not a commitment.

s: "The street" in India refers only to BSE's building.
why: Dalal Street is BSE's address, but "the street" means the market and its professionals.

s: A stock can fall on the day a long-awaited good event happens.
why: Traders who bought the rumour sell once the news arrives.

s: Catching a falling knife means selling a stock before it falls.
why: It means buying a stock that's still dropping sharply, before it has settled.

s: A trader who is long and wrong owns a stock that is falling.
why: They bet on a rise and the market went the other way.

s: Taking some off the table means closing a losing trade.
why: It means selling part of a winning position to lock in gains.

s: Letting winners run often goes with a trailing stop.
why: The stop follows the price up and protects most of the gain.

s: Cutting losers means holding losing trades until they recover.
why: It means exiting losing trades early, at a planned stop.

s: Doubling down usually happens after a position has moved against you.
why: It means making the position much bigger, often after a loss.

s: Scaling in means buying the full position in one order.
why: Scaling in means building the position in steps.

s: Scaling out could mean selling a third of a position at each of three targets.
why: Scaling out is exiting in pieces.

s: "Where's your stop?" asks what profit you expect from the trade.
why: It asks the price at which the idea is wrong and you'll exit.

s: In pyramiding, each addition to a winning position is usually smaller than the last.
why: Adding smaller lots as the price moves your way limits the risk.

s: Revenge trading is a disciplined way to recover losses.
why: It breaks the trader's own rules and usually makes losses bigger.

s: Overtrading raises costs even when the trades break even.
why: Every trade pays brokerage, taxes and spread.

s: A bag holder is the trader who sold at the top.
why: A bag holder is left holding the stock after others sold.

s: The order book shows waiting limit orders, sorted by price.
why: Bids sit on one side, offers on the other.

s: The best bid is always higher than the best offer.
why: In a normal book the best bid sits below the best offer; the gap is the spread.

s: A deep market can absorb a big order without moving the price much.
why: Deep means lots of quantity waiting near the best prices.

s: You can always trade at the mid price with a market order.
why: A market order fills at the bid or offer, not at the mid.

s: The matching engine fills orders by price-time priority.
why: Best price first, then the earliest order at that price.

s: A passive order crosses the spread and trades at once.
why: That's an aggressive order. A passive order waits in the book.

s: An aggressive buy order takes liquidity from the book.
why: It trades at once against orders already waiting.

s: In a thin market, a modest order barely moves the price.
why: Few orders wait, so even modest trades move the price.

s: Auctions like the pre-open session help with price discovery.
why: They pool orders to find one price that reflects them.

s: Market makers earn their profit mainly from commissions charged to clients.
why: They mainly earn the spread between their bid and offer.

s: A market maker trading with better-informed traders faces adverse selection.
why: Informed traders tend to leave the market maker with losses.

s: Informed traders' orders usually carry no information about future prices.
why: Their orders carry real information, which is why market makers fear them.

s: Noise traders give market makers someone to trade with profitably.
why: Their uninformed orders let market makers earn the spread.

s: Algorithmic trading always means trading at very high speed.
why: Algos can be slow, like VWAP over a day. Only HFT is about extreme speed.

s: High-frequency traders often hold positions for seconds or less.
why: Very short holding periods define HFT.

s: Lower latency means orders take longer to reach the exchange.
why: Lower latency means faster: less delay between sending and arriving.

s: Co-location puts a firm's servers inside the exchange's data centre.
why: It cuts the distance, and so the delay, to the matching engine.

s: Slippage only happens with limit orders.
why: It's most common with market orders, which fill wherever the price is.

s: A larger order usually has a higher impact cost.
why: It eats through more price levels in the book.

s: In a call auction, every order fills at its own limit price.
why: All matched orders trade at one price, the one that clears the most quantity.

s: NSE trades some very illiquid stocks only in periodic call auctions.
why: They trade in hourly auctions instead of continuously.

s: Disclosed quantity shows the whole order in market depth.
why: It shows only part of it, revealing more as each part fills.

s: Exchanges can charge traders whose order-to-trade ratio is very high.
why: Too many orders per trade burdens the system, so exchanges penalise it.

s: Algo IDs are optional labels that brokers may add if they wish.
why: Every order from an approved algo must carry its exchange-issued ID.

s: A black-box algo's rules aren't shown to the people using it.
why: That's what black box means; the logic is hidden.

s: Tick-by-tick data gives a snapshot of the market every minute.
why: It records every single order and trade as it happens.

s: Market price protection can leave part of a market order unfilled.
why: It caps how far the order may fill, turning it into a limit order.

s: Spoofing is legal as long as the orders are cancelled in time.
why: Placing orders you never mean to fill, to mislead, is market manipulation.

s: Layering stacks fake orders at several price levels on one side.
why: It's a form of spoofing meant to push the price.

s: Front-running is buying a stock just before your own earnings report.
why: It's trading ahead of a known large order, such as a client's.

s: Trading on unpublished results before they're announced is insider trading.
why: Results are price-sensitive and unpublished, so they're UPSI.

s: UPSI covers any news already published on the exchange website.
why: Once published, it's no longer unpublished; UPSI is news not yet public.

s: A company's trading window closes for insiders from the end of the quarter until results are out.
why: That stops insiders trading on results before the public sees them.

s: Pump-and-dump schemes usually target large, liquid stocks.
why: They target small, thinly traded stocks that are easy to move.

s: Circular trading creates fake volume among related accounts.
why: The group trades the same shares back and forth among themselves.

s: A wash trade changes who owns the shares.
why: The same person is on both sides, so nothing really changes hands.

s: In Indian market slang, an operator is someone who rigs the price of a small stock.
why: Operators use circular trading and tips to move prices.

s: In a lit market, orders are hidden until after they trade.
why: Lit means visible: waiting orders show in the book before they trade.

s: Dark pools let big investors trade size without showing their orders first.
why: Orders aren't displayed before they trade.

s: Fragmentation means all trading in a stock happens on one venue.
why: It means trading is split across several venues.

s: Smart order routing can split an order between NSE and BSE.
why: It sends each part to wherever the best price is.

s: Market makers seek out toxic flow because it pays them the spread.
why: Toxic flow tends to leave the other side with losses; market makers avoid it.

s: Latency arbitrage profits from reacting to price changes before slower traders.
why: Speed lets you trade on prices others haven't updated.

s: Hidden liquidity is shown in full in the order book.
why: By definition it isn't visible in the book.

s: Passive orders usually have lower fill rates than aggressive ones.
why: They wait for a match that may never come.

s: A white-box algo's rules are hidden from users.
why: White-box means the logic is fully shown and can be rebuilt.

s: A retail strategy sending more than 10 orders a second must be registered with the exchange.
why: That's the order-per-second threshold the exchanges set.

s: A static IP changes every time you log in to your broker.
why: Static means fixed: one registered address for API orders.

s: An algo provider offers its algorithms to retail clients through a broker.
why: It builds the algos; the broker makes them available.

s: An index F&O contract can be launched at any value the exchange likes.
why: SEBI sets a minimum value, ₹15 lakh at launch.

s: Brokers must collect the full premium from an option buyer before the order goes in.
why: That's the upfront premium rule.

s: The extra expiry-day margin applies to option buyers.
why: It applies to short options expiring that day.

s: Holding opposite positions in two expiries of the same underlying can lower margin.
why: The positions partly offset, so less margin is needed.

s: Futures-equivalent OI counts every option contract the same, whatever its delta.
why: It weights each option by its delta, measuring risk not contract count.

s: Exchanges check index F&O position limits during the day as well as at the close.
why: They take intraday snapshots to catch limit breaches.

s: A common rule of thumb calls a rise of 20% or more from a low a bull market.
why: It's a rough convention, not a formal definition.

s: A bear market is often defined as a fall of 20% or more from a recent high.
why: That's the common rule of thumb.

s: A rally can happen inside a bear market.
why: Strong rises over days or weeks happen in falling markets too.

s: A sell-off is a slow, gentle decline over many months.
why: A sell-off is a quick, heavy bout of selling.

s: A 12% fall from a recent peak is usually called a correction.
why: Corrections are roughly 10% to 20% falls from a peak.

s: A crash is a gradual slide of about 10% over several months.
why: A crash is a sudden, very steep fall over a day or a few days.

s: A stock at an all-time high has no holders sitting on losses from higher prices.
why: Nobody bought higher, so there's no overhead supply from trapped buyers.

s: A 52-week high is always also an all-time high.
why: It's the highest of the last year; the all-time high may be older and higher.

s: Once support breaks, it often acts as resistance afterwards.
why: Old support becomes a level where sellers show up.

s: Resistance is a price level where falls tend to stop.
why: That's support. Resistance is where rises tend to stall.

s: Traders give more weight to a breakout that comes on heavy volume.
why: Volume suggests real conviction behind the move.

s: In a risk-on mood, investors move money into government bonds and gold.
why: That's risk-off. Risk-on favours shares, small caps and emerging markets.

s: In risk-off phases, money tends to move into government bonds and gold.
why: Investors seek safety.

s: Profit booking can pull prices down even with no bad news.
why: Sellers are locking in gains, not reacting to news.

s: Panic selling is driven by careful analysis of valuations.
why: It's driven by fear, with holdings dumped at almost any price.

s: Capitulation often comes with a spike in volume.
why: The final wave of sellers gives up all at once.

s: FOMO buying is based on careful valuation work.
why: FOMO is buying because others seem to be making money.

s: Buying the dip can hurt badly when a bear market is starting.
why: The fall can keep going instead of recovering.

s: A dead cat bounce is the start of a lasting recovery.
why: It's a brief rebound inside a continuing fall.

s: In a short squeeze, short sellers' buying pushes the price even higher.
why: They buy back to limit losses, adding to the rise.

s: A crowded trade is easy to exit quickly, because so many people hold it.
why: When the story changes everyone rushes for the door, so exits get hard.

s: Selling near the top of a range and buying near the bottom suits a range-bound market.
why: With no trend, prices keep swinging between the same levels.

s: Consolidation is a sharp rise right after a big move.
why: It's a sideways pause after a big move.

s: An uptrend shows higher highs and higher lows.
why: That pattern defines a rising trend.

s: A whipsaw is a long, smooth move in one direction.
why: A whipsaw is a sharp move one way, then a sharp reversal.

s: A gap-up usually follows overnight news or strong global cues.
why: The price opens well above yesterday's close.

s: An overbought stock must fall the next day.
why: Overbought only suggests a pause or pullback is likely; stocks can stay overbought.

s: Indian shares made a V-shaped recovery after the March 2020 crash.
why: Prices fell sharply and rebounded just as fast.

s: A flash crash takes several weeks to recover.
why: A flash crash reverses within minutes.

s: An index can rise while most of its stocks fall.
why: A few heavyweights can carry the index; that's poor breadth.

s: An advance-decline ratio below 1 means more stocks fell than rose.
why: It's rising stocks divided by falling stocks.

s: A broad-based rally is one led by just two or three large stocks.
why: Broad-based means most stocks and sectors rise.

s: Sector rotation can lift banks while IT falls, with the index flat.
why: Money moves between sectors rather than into or out of the market.

s: Cyclical stocks do best during recessions.
why: Their earnings rise and fall with the economy, so they usually suffer in recessions.

s: High-beta stocks tend to fall more than the market in a sell-off.
why: They swing more than the market in both directions.

s: Strong risk appetite shows up as money flowing into gold and government bonds.
why: That's weak risk appetite. Strong appetite sends money into small caps and riskier assets.

s: FPI and DII buying and selling numbers are published every day.
why: They're watched closely as a guide to fund flows.

s: A bubble is easy to recognise and time while it is happening.
why: Bubbles are usually clear only in hindsight.

s: A melt-up is driven more by fear of missing out than by fundamentals.
why: It's a sudden, steep rise late in a bull market.

s: A black swan is a risk everyone expects and prices in.
why: It's a rare, unexpected shock that seems obvious only afterwards.

s: Contagion can make investors sell healthy companies that merely look similar to a troubled one.
why: Fear spreads from one company or market to others.

s: Event risk refers only to surprises nobody can see coming.
why: Event risk is about known events, such as an RBI decision or an election result.

s: A single tariff headline can move a stock sharply within minutes.
why: That's headline risk.

s: In India, all companies report on the same day each quarter.
why: Results come out over a few weeks after each quarter ends.

s: In a liquidity crunch, even good borrowers can struggle to roll over their loans.
why: Cash and credit dry up for almost everyone.

s: De-risking means adding leverage ahead of uncertain events.
why: De-risking means cutting positions and leverage.

s: A price fall with rising open interest suggests fresh short positions.
why: That combination is read as a short build-up.

s: In long unwinding, open interest rises as the price falls.
why: Open interest falls, because longs are closing out.

s: A high delivery percentage suggests buyers are holding shares rather than trading them within the day.
why: It's the share of traded quantity that ends in delivery.

s: Participant-wise OI shows each individual trader's position.
why: It groups positions into clients, DIIs, FIIs and pros.

s: A parent order is usually split into many child orders.
why: The full order is sliced so it can be worked without moving the price.

s: Arrival price is the mid price at the moment the order reached the desk.
why: It's the usual benchmark for implementation shortfall.

s: Brokerage, STT and exchange fees are explicit costs.
why: They're visible on the contract note.

s: The spread you pay and your own market impact are implicit costs.
why: They're hidden in the prices you get, not billed separately.

s: Temporary impact fades after you stop trading.
why: It's the short-lived push from your own buying or selling.

s: Under the square-root law, quadrupling an order's size roughly doubles its impact.
why: Impact grows with the square root of size: √4 = 2.

s: Opportunity cost counts only shares that were actually filled.
why: It's the gain missed on shares that never filled.

s: Trading more slowly lowers timing risk.
why: Trading slowly leaves you exposed to price moves for longer, which raises timing risk.

s: The law of one price says the same asset should trade at the same price everywhere, once costs are counted.
why: Arbitrage closes any gap beyond costs.

s: An ETF's iNAV is its live value worked out from its holdings during the day.
why: Traders compare the ETF's price with iNAV to spot gaps.

s: Leg risk is the danger that one side of an arbitrage fills and the other doesn't.
why: Until both legs fill, you hold a naked position.

s: A signal shared by many traders usually suffers faster alpha decay.
why: Crowding competes the edge away.

s: A market-neutral book aims to make money whether the market rises or falls.
why: Its longs and shorts offset the market's direction.

s: Pairs trading means buying two related stocks together.
why: You buy one and short its close cousin, betting the gap between them closes.

s: Risk parity gives every asset the same amount of money.
why: It weights assets so each adds equal risk, so low-volatility assets get more money.

s: Rolling over a futures position means letting it expire and settle.
why: Rolling over means closing this month's contract and opening the next month's.

s: A bond's coupon changes every day with market yields.
why: For a fixed-rate bond the coupon is set at issue; its price and yield move instead.

s: A bond buyer pays nothing for the interest built up since the last coupon.
why: The buyer pays the seller the accrued interest on top of the price.

s: A hedge using futures on the exact same asset can never have basis risk.
why: The futures-spot gap can still move before expiry, so some basis risk remains.

s: A wider credit spread means the market sees a borrower as safer.
why: A wider spread means investors demand more extra yield, so they see more risk.

s: A dovish central bank leans towards raising rates to fight inflation.
why: That's hawkish. Dovish leans towards lower rates to support growth.

s: Banks earn interest from RBI on the cash they keep as CRR.
why: CRR balances held with the RBI earn no interest.

s: If USDINR rises from 83 to 85, the rupee has strengthened.
why: More rupees per dollar means the rupee has weakened.

s: T-bills pay a coupon twice a year.
why: T-bills are sold at a discount and repaid at face value; there's no coupon.

s: A limit order can sit for hours before it gets a fill.
why: It fills only when someone trades at your price or better.

s: An IOC order never rests in the order book.
why: Whatever can't fill at once is cancelled.

s: You can't buy half a lot of Nifty futures.
why: F&O contracts trade only in whole lots.
